lesson.title: Who Am I? The Adolescent Search for Identity
lesson.summary: Erikson's fifth psychosocial stage centers on adolescence, when the central task is to explore different roles and values and integrate them into a stable sense of identity rather than drifting in confusion about who one is.
lesson.body:
Of Erikson's eight stages, identity versus role confusion is probably the one most people recognize in their own lives, because it corresponds to the stretch of adolescence when questions like what do I believe, what do I want to do, and who am I really start to feel urgent. Erikson described the central task of this stage as integrating the many roles a teenager occupies, student, friend, sibling, romantic partner, worker, into a single, reasonably coherent sense of self. Someone who cannot do this experiences role confusion, a diffuse or unstable identity that makes commitments to values, relationships, or a future path feel unclear or shifting.

This stage depends heavily on developments already underway in adolescence. Cognitively, the emergence of more abstract, hypothetical reasoning gives teenagers a new capacity to think about identity in the first place, to imagine different possible selves and weigh values against each other rather than simply absorbing what adults around them say. Physically and socially, puberty and increasing independence raise the stakes, since the body is changing, peer relationships are becoming more central, and adult decisions about school, work, and relationships are approaching. Identity exploration is, in a real sense, made possible by adolescent development rather than happening in spite of it.

One of the most useful extensions of Erikson's idea came from James Marcia, who operationalized identity development along two dimensions: whether a person has actively explored options, and whether they have made a commitment. Crossing those two produces four identity statuses. Diffusion describes someone who has neither explored nor committed. Foreclosure describes someone who has committed to values or a path, often the ones handed down by parents, without ever really exploring alternatives. Moratorium describes someone actively exploring but not yet committed, which is often treated as a healthy, expected part of the process rather than a problem. Identity achievement describes someone who has explored and reached a committed, examined sense of identity.

It is worth being clear that identity formation is not a single task completed once at eighteen and then finished forever. People often revisit questions of identity at later transitions, a career change, a divorce, a move to a new country, and how much extended identity exploration looks like it varies a good deal across cultures and historical periods, since not every society affords young people the same amount of time and freedom to try on different roles before committing to adult responsibilities.
